headline: Deer Island bunker blitz holds on the new moon push, bluefish riding along for the ride
subhead: I'm staying inside this week — the harbor's peanut bunker show is better than anything the North Shore rocks are giving up right now.
body_markdown:
I had a decision to make Monday morning — run up to Gloucester and work the Cape Ann ledges on the dropping tide, or stay inside the harbor where the bunker's been thick since the weekend. I stayed inside. Wrong call maybe one day out of five, but the numbers said harbor, and the numbers were right.

We flagged this last week — said the dawn blitz pattern in the harbor would hold and that the building new moon current would likely intensify it, and that's exactly what's happened. President Roads and the water off Deer Island Light have had peanut bunker balled up tight against the channel edge every morning this week, with bass busting through them from first light until the sun gets up over the JFK Library. This is mid-August staging behavior — I don't usually see blitz activity this visible in the harbor until the bait starts pushing out in September, but the bunker schools have concentrated the fish hard against structure the whole way from Spectacle Island down through the President Roads channel, and the bass have followed.

Sizes have been mixed but real — plenty of 22 to 28-inch schoolies mixed with a better class of fish, 32 to 36 inches, holding a little deeper on the edges where the bigger bunker are stacked. Best producer's been a simple peanut bunker imitation — 3-inch Albie Snax in bunker color, or a white/chartreuse bucktail worked with a short hop-and-pause through the edge of the bait ball. When the blitz gets tight and visible, a topwater popper thrown right into the froth off Deer Island will draw violent strikes, but don't waste time popping open water — cast to the nervous bait, not the splashes behind it. Outgoing tide has been the best window, roughly two hours either side of the turn, when the current pulls the bunker off the flats and funnels them past the Deer Island rip.

Bluefish are riding shotgun in the same schools, and they're not small — I've seen 3 to 5-pound blues mixed right in with the stripers off Spectacle Island, which tells me the adult class fish are building the way they usually do this time of year behind a good peanut bunker push. If you're getting bit off and missing hookups on soft plastics, that's your blues — switch to a wire leader or a metal lure like a Kastmaster and you'll start connecting instead of losing gear.

Nahant's been a mixed bag. The rocks off East Point and the ledges running out toward Egg Rock are still holding bass, but it's been more of a north-shore grind than a blitz — one or two fish on a tide, mostly on the last two hours of the incoming when water pushes bait up against the structure. Live mackerel under a slip float has out-produced everything else out there this week, and mackerel themselves have been easy to jig up on Diamond jigs and Swedish Pimples in 20 to 30 feet right off the point, so bait's not the problem — it's just that the bass have their attention locked on the harbor's bunker right now and the North Shore rocks are getting the leftovers.

Gloucester and Cape Ann have been quieter on the striper front, but that's typical for mid-August — the better story up there right now is mackerel and the early groundfish grind. Cod and haddock are still around the deeper water off Cape Ann, but you're working 60 to 90 feet with jigs or clams on the bottom for a mixed bag rather than a sure thing, and I wouldn't plan a trip around it this week.

South of the city, Plymouth and Duxbury Bay are part of the same story running up the coast — bunker-driven bass activity has been showing from Narragansett clear up into Cape Cod Bay, and Plymouth's no exception. Duxbury Bay and the flats around Kingston Bay have flounder moving well on the low tide — small strips of clam or squid on a simple flounder rig in 8 to 12 feet of water over mud bottom has been steady, not spectacular, but a good option on a day when the bass bite's slow. Scituate's rocky shoreline has given up a few bass on the same live mackerel program that's working at Nahant, best fished on the last of the incoming right up against the ledges.

Wind's been light out of the southwest most mornings, which has kept the harbor calm enough to work the bunker schools without getting bounced around, and that's part of why the blitz has stayed so visible and workable. If that holds through the weekend and the bunker don't push out of the harbor, I'd keep working the Deer Island to Spectacle Island stretch on the outgoing tide — that's still the highest-percentage program in my zone. If the wind swings onshore and stirs things up, I'd shift south to Duxbury Bay and fish the flounder on the calmer water while waiting for the harbor to settle back down. Either way, keep an eye out to the south — there's real talk of the first false albacore or bonito of the season showing somewhere between here and Buzzards Bay in the next few days, and if that bait and warm water pattern keeps pushing north, Plymouth could be the first place in my zone to see one.
